title: Earth Systems, Plate Tectonics and Rocks
seo_title: Year 11 Earth and Environmental Science: Earth Systems and the Geosphere Worksheets
standard_code: Earth and Environmental Science Unit 1: Earth systems and the development of the geosphere
standard_text: The Earth system model (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere), open and closed systems, reservoirs, fluxes and feedback; Earth's layers and their evidence; plate tectonics; rocks, minerals and the rock cycle; relative and radiometric dating. (Senior Secondary Earth and Environmental Science, Unit 1: Introduction to Earth systems)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Earth and Environmental Science worksheets on Earth systems: the four spheres, feedback loops, Earth's layers, seismic evidence, plate tectonics, rocks and radiometric dating. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth's four spheres exchange matter and energy.
key_sub: Positive feedback amplifies change; negative feedback reduces it.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Earth system has four spheres: geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere. Matter moves between reservoirs as fluxes; feedback loops can amplify (positive) or dampen (negative) a change.

Early Earth melted and separated into a dense iron core, a mantle and a light crust. Seismic waves reveal the layers: S-waves cannot cross the liquid outer core. The lithosphere is broken into plates moved by mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull.

Rocks are igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic and change through the rock cycle. Superposition gives relative ages; radiometric dating gives absolute ages. Western Australia's Jack Hills zircons are about 4.4 billion years old.

Example

A rock has 25% of its parent isotope left (half-life 700 million years). Age?

25% = 2 half-lives

2 × 700 million

Answer: 1.4 billion years

Example

A plate moves 7 cm per year. How far in 1 million years?

7 × 1000 000 cm = 7000 000 cm

Answer: 70 km

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the whole mantle is liquid: it is solid rock that flows very slowly.
  • Calling every feedback ‘bad’: positive means amplifying, not good.
  • Confusing relative dating (order) with absolute dating (age in years).

faq.q: How do we know what is inside Earth?
faq.a: Mostly from seismic waves: their speeds change at boundaries, and S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core. Meteorites and lab experiments add evidence.

faq.q: Why are the Jack Hills zircons important?
faq.a: At about 4.4 billion years they are the oldest known pieces of Earth, and show that crust, and probably water, existed very early.

items.q: Melting sea ice exposes dark ocean, which absorbs more sunlight and melts more ice. What is this?
items.e: Positive feedback amplifies the change.

items.q: What is a flux in an Earth system model?
c: the rate at which matter or energy moves between reservoirs
items.e: Evaporation is a flux from ocean to atmosphere.

items.q: Earth is usually described as a closed system. What does this mean?
c: it is not affected by the Sun
it exchanges lots of matter with space
it exchanges energy with space but almost no matter
items.e: Meteorites and escaping gases are tiny amounts.

items.q: Warmer oceans evaporate more water, and water vapour is a greenhouse gas that causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a closed loop with no effect
items.e: The water vapour feedback amplifies warming.

items.q: Warmer air holds more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: A dam is built across a river. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: A hotter Earth gives off more infrared energy to space, which cools it down. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Drought kills plants, so less water evaporates from leaves, so less rain falls, making the drought worse. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Warming thaws permafrost, which releases methane, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Which statement about energy and matter in the Earth system is correct?
c: matter flows in from the Sun
energy flows through the system from the Sun and out to space, while matter is mostly recycled
matter is lost to space quickly
items.e: Earth is close to a closed system for matter.

items.q: Which sphere includes all living things?
items.e: It overlaps with the other three spheres.

items.q: A city paves over a large area. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the geosphere and hydrosphere (coasts erode faster without reefs)
the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Termites build mounds and mix soil in northern Australia. Which spheres interact?
c: the hydrosphere and the atmosphere only
items.e: Living things change soils.

items.q: What is a limitation of a box-and-arrow model of the water cycle?
c: it simplifies the system and may leave out how fluxes change over time and place
items.e: Models must be judged by how well they explain data.

items.q: Which sphere includes all of Earth's water, including ice and groundwater?
items.e: Ice is sometimes called the cryosphere.

items.q: What does dynamic equilibrium mean for an Earth system?
c: inputs and outputs balance so the system stays about the same even though matter keeps moving
the system is always changing quickly
inputs are always larger than outputs
items.e: A stable lake has inflows that balance outflows.

items.q: Beavers build dams in a valley. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the geosphere and hydrosphere (coasts erode faster without reefs)
the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Heavy rain falls on bare hills. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: More rainfall speeds up rock weathering, which removes CO₂ from the air over long times. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: More prey lets predators increase, and the predators then reduce the prey. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Evidence: Earth's average density (5.5 g/cm³) is much greater than crust rock (2.7 g/cm³). What does it show?
c: The outer core is a different material and state from the mantle.
A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
Much denser material, like iron, must be deep inside.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's crust?
c: thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents
rigid outer layer of crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates
solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure
thick layer of hot solid rock that moves by slow convection
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: About how fast is the Australian plate moving north?
items.e: Australia's GPS coordinates are updated because of this.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's inner core?
c: thick layer of hot solid rock that moves by slow convection
liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field
solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure
rigid outer layer of crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: How does a metamorphic rock form?
c: an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting
items.e: Shale becomes slate; limestone becomes marble.

items.q: What forms where two oceanic plates move apart?
c: a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
items.e: Magma rises to fill the gap.

items.q: What is a mineral?
c: a substance made by living things
a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure
items.e: Quartz is SiO₂.

items.q: About how old is Earth?
items.e: 13.8 billion years is the age of the universe.

items.q: How did Earth's layers form?
c: the crust formed first and then the core
they were all added by meteorites in order
early Earth was hot enough to melt, so dense iron sank to form the core and lighter rock rose
items.e: This separation is called differentiation.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's asthenosphere?
c: thick layer of hot solid rock that moves by slow convection
hot, soft part of the upper mantle that flows slowly
thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents
rigid outer layer of crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: Evidence: Seismic waves slow down in a zone about 100–200 km deep. What does it show?
c: Much denser material, like iron, must be deep inside.
A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's outer core?
c: liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field
solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure
rigid outer layer of crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates
hot, soft part of the upper mantle that flows slowly
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: Which process turns loose sediment into sedimentary rock?
items.e: Minerals cement the grains together.

items.q: Which layer is described: thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents?
items.e: Layers differ in composition and state.

items.q: Evidence: There is a shadow zone where no direct S waves arrive. What does it show?
c: The outer core is a different material and state from the mantle.
Much denser material, like iron, must be deep inside.
A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: Which evidence supports this claim: “A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.”
c: S waves do not pass through the outer core.
There is a shadow zone where no direct S waves arrive.
P waves bend and slow down when they enter the outer core.
Earth's average density (5.5 g/cm³) is much greater than crust rock (2.7 g/cm³).
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: A basalt dyke cuts through sandstone layers. Which is younger?
items.e: Principle of cross-cutting relationships.

items.q: Evidence: P waves speed up again in the inner core. What does it show?
c: A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's mantle?
c: hot, soft part of the upper mantle that flows slowly
solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure
thick layer of hot solid rock that moves by slow convection
liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: Which evidence supports this claim: “The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.”
c: Earth's average density (5.5 g/cm³) is much greater than crust rock (2.7 g/cm³).
P waves speed up again in the inner core.
Seismic waves slow down in a zone about 100–200 km deep.
There is a shadow zone where no direct S waves arrive.
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): the Alpine Fault in New Zealand.

items.q: Which statement about the age of oceanic crust is correct?
c: it is oldest at mid-ocean ridges
it is older than most continental crust
it is the same age everywhere
it is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and gets older away from them
items.e: Oceanic crust is rarely older than about 200 million years.

items.q: A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 6 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 4 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Which kind of plate boundary forms the Alpine Fault in New Zealand?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Mei finds seafloor rock 240 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 4 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 240 km = 24000000 cm; ÷ 4 million years = 6 cm/yr.

items.q: Priya finds seafloor rock 80 km from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is 4 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 80 km = 8000000 cm; ÷ 4 million years = 2 cm/yr.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: fold mountains such as the Himalayas
sudden earthquakes along a fault line
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): fold mountains such as the Himalayas.

items.q: Kai finds seafloor rock 500 km from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is 20 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 500 km = 50000000 cm; ÷ 20 million years = 2.5 cm/yr.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 6 cm per year. About how old is rock 3000 km from the ridge?
Why does granite have larger crystals than basalt?
c: granite cooled slowly underground, giving crystals time to grow
granite cooled quickly at the surface
items.e: Fast cooling at the surface gives small crystals.

items.q: How do we know the outer core is liquid?
c: S-waves (shear waves) do not travel through it, leaving an S-wave shadow zone
items.e: P-waves pass through but are refracted.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a divergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: divergent (plates move apart): Iceland splitting slowly apart.

items.q: Noah finds seafloor rock 2000 km from a mid-ocean ridge that is 50 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 2000 km = 200000000 cm; ÷ 50 million years = 4 cm/yr.

items.q: What do 4.4-billion-year-old zircons tell us about early Earth?
c: there was continental crust and probably liquid water very early
Earth had no crust for 2 billion years
items.e: Their oxygen isotopes suggest they formed with water present.

items.q: A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 5 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 20 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Seafloor spreads at 4 cm per year. About how old is rock 1600 km from the ridge?
A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 10 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 40 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Which kind of plate boundary forms deep ocean trenches?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: A plate moves away from a mid-ocean ridge at 4 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 40 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
What are the three main types of rock?
items.e: The rock cycle links them.

sets.title: Rocks, minerals and the rock cycle

items.q: How did the rock of Kata Tjuta form?
c: from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
from layers of river sand pressed together
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
items.e: Kata Tjuta is conglomerate (sedimentary).

items.q: Uluru is made of arkose. What type of rock is it?
items.e: The layers were tilted almost vertical by earth movements.

items.q: What forms where an oceanic plate subducts beneath another plate?
c: a deep trench and a chain of volcanoes
items.e: The Pacific 'Ring of Fire' has many subduction zones.

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the Moon forms after a giant impact?
c: They happened at the same time.
oxygen begins to build up in the air
the Moon forms after a giant impact
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the Moon forms after a giant impact, or the first animals appear?
c: the Moon forms after a giant impact
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: What kind of rock is the slate roofs of old Adelaide houses made of?
items.e: It formed from mudstone changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
oxygen begins to build up in the air
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: What kind of rock is Wave Rock in Western Australia made of?
items.e: It formed from magma that cooled slowly deep underground.

items.q: How did the rock of Uluru form?
c: from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
from mudstone changed by heat and pressure
items.e: Uluru is arkose, a sandstone (sedimentary).

items.q: Which type of plate boundary is the Alpine Fault in New Zealand, where plates slide past each other?
items.e: Transform boundaries cause large earthquakes.

items.q: How did the rock of Sydney's harbour cliffs form?
c: from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from mudstone changed by heat and pressure
from layers of river sand pressed together
items.e: Sydney's harbour cliffs is Hawkesbury sandstone (sedimentary).

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts: about 4 billion years ago.

items.q: What kind of rock is Uluru made of?
items.e: It formed from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or oxygen begins to build up in the air?
c: They happened at the same time.
oxygen begins to build up in the air
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: What drives the movement of tectonic plates?
c: mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull
the rotation of the core only
items.e: Slab pull at subduction zones is the strongest force.

items.q: What kind of rock is the Organ Pipes in Victoria made of?
items.e: It formed from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns.

items.q: Which happened first: the first animals appear, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: What evidence supports continental drift?
c: matching fossils (such as Glossopteris), rocks and glacial deposits on continents that are now far apart
all continents have the same climate
items.e: Australia, Antarctica, Africa and the other southern landmasses were joined in Gondwana.

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: oxygen begins to build up in the air
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the first microbial fossils (stromatolites), or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago.

items.q: A rock has uranium-235 and lead-207 in a ratio of 1 : 3 (half-life of uranium-235: 704 million years). How old is it? (Assume all the lead-207 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 3 means 1/4 is left → 2 half-lives = 1408 million years.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
items.e: S-waves cannot travel through it.

items.q: Which sphere does the ozone layer belong to?
items.e: It is in the stratosphere.

items.q: How does an igneous rock form?
c: by heat and pressure changing another rock without melting
by layers of sediment being cemented
by magma or lava cooling and crystallising
items.e: Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.q: A rock has potassium-40 and argon-40 in a ratio of 1 : 3 (half-life of potassium-40: 1.25 billion years). How old is it? (Assume all the argon-40 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 3 means 1/4 is left → 2 half-lives = 2.5 billion years.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/64 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5730 years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/64 = 6 half-lives; 6 × 5730 = 34380 years.

items.q: Which rock is formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms?
items.e: Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate.

items.q: Where in Australia have the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust (zircon crystals about 4.4 billion years old) been found?
c: the Jack Hills in Western Australia
the Blue Mountains in New South Wales
items.e: Zircons are very resistant and can be dated with uranium–lead dating.

items.q: A sample starts with 128 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 3 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 3 times: 16 g.

items.q: A mineral has 1/8 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/8 = 3 half-lives; 3 × 704 = 2112 million years.

items.q: A sample starts with 64 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 3 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 3 times: 8 g.

items.q: A mineral has 1/64 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/64 = 6 half-lives; 6 × 704 = 4224 million years.

items.q: A sample had 32 g of parent and now has 8 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 32 → 8 takes 2 halvings.

items.q: A sample had 100 g of parent and now has 12.5 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 100 → 12.5 takes 3 halvings.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of Earth systems?
c: because models are always exactly right
to simplify complex systems so they can be explained and predictions tested
items.e: All models have limitations.

items.q: A rock started with 320 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 2 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 320 − 80 = 240 g.

items.q: A mineral has 1/4 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/4 = 2 half-lives; 2 × 704 = 1408 million years.

items.q: A rock started with 80 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 2 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 80 − 20 = 60 g.

items.q: What is the principle of superposition?
c: the youngest layers are at the bottom
in undisturbed sedimentary layers, the lowest layers are the oldest
all layers formed at the same time
items.e: It gives relative ages.

items.q: A rock started with 64 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 2 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 64 − 16 = 48 g.
